text: You've read an English sentence up to one hidden character. With yes or no questions, how many do you need per character on average? The natural answer is 5. Each answer can cut what's left in half, and 5 cuts take 27 down to 1. The ideal is log base 2 of 27, about 4.75. In 1951, Claude Shannon estimated the true figure at about 1. Whatever it is, no text compressor can beat it on average, and guessing what comes next is how language models are trained. So where do four of every five questions go? Splitting the alphabet evenly charges every character the same price. Z costs as much as E, yet E turns up 130 times as often. Instead, ask questions that split the probability, not the alphabet. Is it a space, E, T, A, or O? Those five make up nearly half of all text. E starts near a tenth of the bar. Each ideal answer keeps half the probability, so E doubles its share of what's left. 3.3 ideal doublings, and E fills the whole bar. Z starts at 1 in 1260, and needs 10.3. In general, a character with probability P needs K questions, where P times 2 to the k equals 1. So 2 to the k equals 1 over p, and k equals log base 2 of 1 over p. Now give each character its own cost as a height. The widths add up to 1, so the total area is the average number of questions per character. Pour the skyline flat, and its height is that average Shannon called that average the entropy counted in bits 1 bit per yes or no answer For English letters it 4 That beats 4 but it still four times Shannon estimate It prices every character as if nothing came before it What comes after a Q? It's U, 98 times out of 100. U swallows the bar. Its cost drops to almost nothing, and the average falls to 0.16 bits. After th, e takes two-thirds of the bar, and its cost shrinks to about half a question. Half a question, like 3.3 doublings, sounds impossible, but a compressor asks about long runs of letters, and the fractions add up. After th, the average is 1.7, but averaged over every two-letter context, it's still 2.8. Some contexts need more text than any corpus holds, so Shannon used a predictor that already knows English. A person. His subject read a passage letter by letter, guessing each next one until right. 79 of 102 came on the first guess. A twin who guesses the same way could rebuild the passage from these counts alone. Treat each guess count as a symbol, and the same skyline pores, flat at about 1.4 bits. A better guesser could only lower it. Shannon's tests, with 100 letters of context, put English between 0.6 and 1.3 bits per character. In 2023, a language model compressing part of a book that reached Project Gutenberg after its training, in the same 27 symbols, needed 0.84 bits, inside that range. The hidden character from the start is the Y at the end of the other day. Shannon's subject got it on the first guess, a single yes or no question. Splitting the alphabet took five. In English, almost no letter arrives without a past.
